origins: Invisible pain and unpredictable symptoms leave room for doubt. Remarks like “But you look fine,” or being accused of attention-seeking, hurt deeply. Some patients start hiding symptoms or over-explaining to prove they are sick.
teaches: Job’s friends accused him of hidden sin instead of believing his pain, and God rebuked them for not speaking about Him accurately, as His servant Job had (Job 42:7). Jesus had compassion on the suffering and never demanded that they prove it. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.” “Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” God sees what others cannot, and some people will believe you.
self_statements: I have to prove I am sick.
I cannot explain what it is like.
errors: Believing people either see my pain or think I am faking.
Feeling doubted and concluding that everyone doubts me.
questions: Who believes me, even if only a few?
What do I want others to understand?
How do I feel when I over-explain?
How could I set a boundary with people who doubt?
Who might benefit from a patient-support group?
truth: God sees and knows my suffering, and Jesus sympathizes. I do not have to prove my pain to everyone. I can find those who believe me and set kind boundaries with those who do not.
hw_truths: I do not have to prove my pain.
log: Each week, note one person who believed or supported you.
actions: Write those who take you seriously.
Write one line for explaining your condition.
prayer: Lord, others doubt my pain, but You know it fully. Give me peace, supportive people, and grace to set boundaries. Amen.
